/rent-to-own.title: Rent To Own Homes in Colorado: Loveland, Fort Collins, Greeley & Northern Colorado
/rent-to-own.metaDescription: How rent-to-own really works in Colorado — who it helps, what it costs, the scams to avoid, and the $0-down programs many renters qualify for instead. Straight answers from a Loveland Realtor.

sections.h2: How does rent-to-own actually work in Colorado?
paragraphs: A rent-to-own agreement is really two contracts in one: a normal lease, plus either an option to purchase (you CAN buy at a set price later) or a purchase agreement (you're committing to buy). You'll typically pay an up-front option fee and sometimes a monthly premium above market rent, with some portion credited toward the purchase if — and only if — you close.

The fine print decides everything. Who handles repairs during the rental period? What happens to your option fee and rent credits if you can't qualify for a mortgage when the option comes due? In most agreements the honest answer is: you lose them. That's why I tell people to treat rent-to-own as a financing bridge with a deadline, not a soft version of buying.

In Northern Colorado, true rent-to-own inventory is thin — most sellers can sell outright, so they have little reason to offer terms. The listings that do exist deserve extra scrutiny, and the ones that sound too easy usually are. I've written a town-by-town breakdown for [Loveland](/rent-to-own-in-loveland) and [Fort Collins](/rent-to-own-in-fort-collins) if you're searching in a specific market.

sections.h2: What credit score do you need for rent-to-own?
paragraphs: There's no fixed score — the landlord-seller sets the bar, which is exactly why rent-to-own attracts people who've been told 'no' by a lender. But here's the part most renters are never told: the mortgage you'll need at the END of the rental period has real qualifying standards, and if your credit isn't mortgage-ready by then, the deal fails and the extra money you paid is usually gone.

Most buyers I work with who start below a 620 score are mortgage-ready within about four to six months of focused work — often faster than a rent-to-own term. That path keeps your money in your own pocket instead of a seller's option fee.

sections.h2: Rent-to-own vs. low- and zero-down programs: which actually gets you a home?
paragraphs: Before signing a rent-to-own contract, check what you already qualify for. Colorado has real down-payment help — CHFA down-payment assistance, the Metro DPA program, VA loans with $0 down for veterans, USDA loans with $0 down in rural towns like Severance, Wellington, Ault, and Eaton — and program details and amounts change, so ask us to verify what's current for your situation.

For a lot of the renters who land on this page, one of those programs beats every rent-to-own deal on the market: you own the home now, at today's price, with your payments building your own equity. Take the [60-second readiness check at OwnInNoCo](https://owninnoco.com) — it's my first-time-buyer hub, and it maps which path fits you.

sections.h2: Rent-to-own scams: the red flags
paragraphs: The rent-to-own space attracts scammers because it targets people who feel out of options. Walk away from: anyone demanding a large non-refundable fee before you've seen a contract, 'sellers' who won't prove they hold title (a quick county records search shows the real owner), contracts where any late rent payment voids your entire option and credits, and prices set far above what the home is worth — a baked-in failure, because no lender will appraise it there when you go to buy.

Have a real estate agent or attorney read any rent-to-own contract before you sign. I do this for Northern Colorado renters regularly, no charge and no pressure — it's a fifteen-minute conversation that can save you a five-figure mistake.

faq: How does rent-to-own work in Colorado?

You lease the home while holding either an option or an obligation to buy it at a set price, usually paying an up-front option fee and monthly credits that apply only if you close. Colorado has no special rent-to-own statute protecting your credits, so the contract terms are everything — have someone qualified read them before you sign.
Is rent-to-own a good idea for bad credit?

Sometimes — but usually only if you have a concrete plan to be mortgage-ready before the option expires. If your credit can't qualify for the purchase loan at the end, you typically lose the option fee and rent credits. Many renters below a 620 score can become mortgage-ready in months and buy outright instead.
Are there rent-to-own homes in Loveland or Fort Collins right now?

True rent-to-own listings in Northern Colorado are rare and change constantly — most sellers simply sell. The reliable path is telling me what you're looking for; I'll flag genuine lease-option opportunities and, just as often, show you a zero- or low-down path to owning outright.
What's the difference between a lease-option and a lease-purchase?

A lease-option gives you the right to buy — you can walk away, losing your fee. A lease-purchase obligates you to buy, and walking away can put you in breach of contract. Know which one you're signing before money changes hands.
What programs help if I can't save a down payment?

Colorado buyers use CHFA down-payment assistance, Metro DPA, VA loans ($0 down for eligible veterans), and USDA loans ($0 down in qualifying rural areas of Weld and Larimer counties). Amounts and eligibility change — ask us to verify what's current before you count on a number.
Who pays for repairs in a rent-to-own home?

Whatever the contract says — and many shift maintenance onto the tenant-buyer even though the seller still owns the home. That's one of the first clauses I check when a renter brings me an agreement to review.

/rent-to-own-in-fort-collins.title: Rent To Own Homes in Fort Collins, CO: What's Real & What To Do Instead
/rent-to-own-in-fort-collins.metaDescription: Looking for rent-to-own homes in Fort Collins? Here's what actually exists, what the contracts hide, and the zero-down paths many Fort Collins renters qualify for instead.

sections.h2: Are there really rent-to-own homes in Fort Collins?
paragraphs: Genuine rent-to-own listings in Fort Collins are scarce — in a market where sellers can sell outright, few offer terms, and many of the 'rent to own Fort Collins' results you'll see online are lead traps or listings that expired long ago. When a real lease-option does appear, it's usually a homeowner in an unusual situation, and the contract deserves professional review before any money moves.

If you're renting in Fort Collins and the mortgage math feels out of reach, the more common success story I see is a renter who discovers they qualify for more help than they thought — CHFA assistance, Metro DPA, VA or USDA depending on eligibility and location. Program details change; ask us to verify what's current. Start with the [honest rent-to-own guide](/rent-to-own) or the [readiness check at OwnInNoCo](https://owninnoco.com).

faq: How do I find legitimate rent-to-own homes in Fort Collins?

Work with a local agent who can separate real lease-option offers from recycled internet bait. I watch the Fort Collins market daily and will tell you plainly when something genuine appears — and when nothing currently is, which is often the truth.
What does rent-to-own cost up front in Fort Collins?

Typically an option fee set by the seller plus above-market rent with credits toward purchase. Both are negotiable and both are usually forfeited if you don't close — which is why comparing that cost against a low-down-payment purchase first is worth thirty minutes of your time.
Can I buy in Fort Collins with a low credit score instead?

Often, yes — or within a few months of focused credit work. Many renters who assume they need rent-to-own qualify for FHA, VA, or CHFA-assisted loans sooner than they expect. It costs nothing to find out where you actually stand.
Is rent-to-own better than renting while I fix my credit?

Only if the contract genuinely protects your credits and the purchase price is fair. Otherwise plain renting plus a credit plan leaves you freer and usually richer — you keep your money and your options.

/rent-to-own-in-loveland.title: Rent To Own Homes in Loveland, CO: An Honest Local Guide
/rent-to-own-in-loveland.metaDescription: Rent-to-own homes in Loveland: what actually exists, how the contracts work, the scams to avoid, and the low- and zero-down alternatives Loveland renters use to buy outright.

sections.h2: What rent-to-own looks like in Loveland right now
paragraphs: Loveland is my home market — I live here, and I watch it daily. True lease-option listings come up rarely, and when they do the terms vary wildly, because each one is a private seller writing their own rules. A fair one can genuinely bridge a renter into ownership; an unfair one quietly collects your option fee and hands the home to the next hopeful tenant when your financing falls through.

The full picture — how the contracts work, the credit question, the scams, and the down-payment programs that often beat rent-to-own entirely — is in my [Colorado rent-to-own guide](/rent-to-own). If you're set on Loveland specifically, tell me what you're looking for and I'll tell you what's real this week, including homes where a seller might entertain terms even if the listing doesn't say so.

faq: Are there rent-to-own homes in Loveland right now?

Inventory changes weekly and true lease-options are rare — most Loveland sellers sell outright. The dependable route is telling me your budget and timeline; I'll flag anything genuine and show you the buy-outright paths you may already qualify for.
What should a fair Loveland rent-to-own contract include?

A purchase price tied to a real appraisal, clearly stated option fees and rent credits, a rental period long enough for your financing plan, and repair responsibilities that stay with the owner. I review these contracts for Loveland renters at no charge.
Can first-time buyers in Loveland get down-payment help instead?

Frequently, yes — CHFA assistance and Metro DPA serve Loveland buyers, VA loans offer $0 down for eligible veterans, and nearby towns qualify for USDA $0-down. Amounts and rules change, so ask us to verify what's current for you.
What credit score do I need to buy in Loveland?

Lower than most renters assume for FHA and some CHFA-assisted paths, and many buyers below 620 become mortgage-ready within months. Where you are today matters less than having the plan — that's a free conversation.

/what-is-an-ilc-and-when-should-you-get-.title: What Is an ILC? Improvement Location Certificate vs. Survey, Cost & When You Need One
/what-is-an-ilc-and-when-should-you-get-.metaDescription: ILC meaning in Colorado real estate: what an Improvement Location Certificate shows, how it differs from a boundary survey, roughly what each costs, and when a lender requires one.

sections.h2: What is an ILC in real estate?
paragraphs: An ILC — Improvement Location Certificate — is a Colorado-specific document in which a licensed surveyor certifies, based on a visual inspection and existing records, where the improvements (house, garage, fences, driveway) appear to sit relative to the property's boundaries and any easements. It's the quick sanity check of Colorado closings: does anything obviously encroach, and does the legal description match what's on the ground?

What an ILC is NOT is a boundary survey. The surveyor doesn't set or verify property corners for an ILC, and the certificate itself says it can't be relied on to build a fence, settle a boundary dispute, or locate exact lines. It answers 'does anything look wrong here?' — not 'exactly where is my line?'

sections.h2: How much does an ILC cost in Colorado?
paragraphs: An ILC is one of the cheapest pieces of a Colorado closing — typically a small fraction of the cost of a full boundary survey, because the surveyor isn't setting corners or doing full field measurement. Exact pricing varies by company, county, parcel size, and turnaround time, so get a current quote for your specific property rather than trusting a number from an article — including this one.

A full boundary or Improvement Survey Plat costs meaningfully more and takes longer, which is why lenders and title companies in Colorado usually ask for just the ILC on a typical town-lot purchase — and why buyers of acreage, unfenced land, or anything with a boundary question should seriously consider paying for the real survey anyway. On rural land, the survey is cheap insurance against the most expensive kind of neighbor disagreement.

sections.h2: When does a lender require an ILC — and when should you insist on more?
paragraphs: In most Colorado purchase transactions the title company or lender orders an ILC to check for obvious encroachments before issuing title insurance. It's routine on subdivision lots where corners are well established and recent surveys exist.

Insist on a full survey instead when you're buying [rural land or acreage](/buying-land-larimer-co), when fences don't obviously match the legal description, when a seller can't say where the corners are, when you plan to build near a setback, or when any neighbor has ever disagreed about a line. If you're weighing that call on a specific Northern Colorado property, ask me — I'll tell you honestly which document the situation deserves.

faq: What does ILC stand for in real estate?

Improvement Location Certificate — a Colorado surveyor's certification of where the improvements on a property appear to sit relative to boundaries and easements, used by lenders and title companies as a closing-time sanity check.
What's the difference between an ILC and a survey?

An ILC is a visual check that doesn't establish property corners and legally can't be relied on to locate exact boundary lines. A boundary survey sets or verifies the corners and is the document you need for fences, building, or disputes.
How much does an ILC cost in Colorado?

Substantially less than a boundary survey — it's usually one of the smaller line items at closing. Prices vary by surveyor, county, and parcel, so get a current quote for your property; any specific dollar figure you read online may be stale.
Do I need an ILC when buying a house in Colorado?

Your lender or title company usually decides — most order one on standard purchases. Buyers of acreage or any property with unclear lines should consider upgrading to a full survey regardless of what the lender minimally requires.
Can I use an ILC to build a fence?
No — the certificate itself disclaims that use. Building on or near what you think is your line without a real survey is how boundary disputes start. Spend the money on the survey first.

sections.h2: Where the Larimer County Land Use Code fits in
paragraphs: Open zoning is defined in the Larimer County Land Use Code — the county's rulebook for what every unincorporated parcel can and can't do. The code sets each zone district's permitted uses, minimum lot sizes, setbacks, and the review processes (like site plan review or special review) that certain uses trigger. If your parcel is outside city limits in Larimer County, this code — not Fort Collins' or Loveland's municipal rules — is what governs it.

Two practical steps before you buy or build: look up your parcel's exact zoning on the county's online property records, and read the current Land Use Code section for that district at larimer.gov — the county updates the code, so a summary you read elsewhere (including this page) is a starting point, never the final word. When a plan matters, a call to Larimer County Planning with your parcel number gets you an answer specific to your land.

If you're comparing parcels or getting ready to act on one, I walk buyers and sellers through this regularly — what the zoning realistically allows, which questions to put to Planning, and what it means for the land's value. Details on the buying-and-selling side are in my companion guide to [open zoning when buying or selling land in Larimer County](/open-zoning-buying-selling-land-larimer).

faq: What does O zoning mean in Larimer County?

O is the county's Open zone district, common on rural and foothills land — it allows uses like single-family homes and agriculture at low density, with large minimum lot sizes and restrictions that preserve the area's rural character. The exact permitted-use list lives in the Larimer County Land Use Code.
Can you build a house on open-zoned land?

Generally yes — a single-family home is a typical permitted use — subject to the district's minimum lot size, setbacks, and the county's building and septic/well permitting. Verify your specific parcel with Larimer County Planning before you count on it.
What is the minimum lot size in Larimer County open zoning?

Open zoning carries large minimums, and the current figure and its exceptions come from the Land Use Code, which the county amends over time. Check the code section for the O district or ask Planning with your parcel number — don't rely on a cached number from an article.
Where do I find the Larimer County Land Use Code?

On larimer.gov under the Community Development / Planning pages, alongside the county's zoning maps and property lookup tools. The code plus your parcel's zoning designation together answer most of what a buyer needs to know.
Does open zoning allow horses or livestock?

Agricultural uses including keeping animals are typical in the O district, with the specifics — how many, and any use review triggers — set by the code. If horse property is the goal, I can help you confirm a parcel supports it before you write an offer.

sections.h2: Buying or selling open-zoned land? Start with these three checks
paragraphs: First, pull the parcel's zoning and any recorded easements from Larimer County's property records — what a listing says and what the county says are occasionally two different things, and only one of them is binding. Second, read the current Land Use Code for the O district (my [plain-English open zoning explainer](/understanding-open-zoning-in-larimer-county) covers what to look for). Third, before pricing or offering, get clear on water and septic: a parcel that can't get a well permit or won't perc for septic is a very different asset than its acreage suggests.

Sellers: buyers of open-zoned land are buying what's POSSIBLE, so documentation is your marketing. A recent survey, well records, septic history, and a written summary of what the zoning allows will earn you offers that hold together. I prepare exactly that package when I list rural land — it's a big part of why those listings close instead of falling apart in due diligence.

faq: Does open zoning make land worth more or less?

It depends what a buyer wants to do. The low density that limits development also protects the rural character many buyers are paying for. Value comes from the specific parcel's buildability — water, septic, access, and what the code allows — more than the zone label itself.
Can open-zoned land be subdivided in Larimer County?

Sometimes, through county processes with real requirements and timelines — and sometimes effectively not. The answer is parcel-specific; get it from the Land Use Code and a conversation with county Planning before you buy on the assumption.
What should I disclose when selling open-zoned land?

Everything material you know: water and mineral rights status, easements, past permits or denials, septic and well history. Beyond legal obligation, full documentation is what makes rural land sales close — surprises in title work kill them.

/whats-the-real-cost-to-develop-raw-land.title: How Much Does It Cost To Develop Raw Land in Colorado? Water, Power, Septic & Access
/whats-the-real-cost-to-develop-raw-land.metaDescription: What it really costs to get water, electricity, septic, and a driveway onto raw Colorado land — how each is priced, what drives the number up, and the questions that get you real quotes.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to get water to a property?
paragraphs: Water is usually the most consequential development question in Colorado, and it's priced two completely different ways. If a water district serves your road, you'll pay a tap fee set by that district — each district publishes its own fee schedule, they differ enormously across Northern Colorado, and they change, so the district's current schedule is the only number that counts. If no district line reaches you, you're drilling a well: pricing is per-foot plus pump and equipment, so depth to water drives everything, and only local well drillers who know the area's geology can quote it honestly.

Before any of that: confirm the parcel's water rights and what kind of well permit Colorado's Division of Water Resources would issue for it. In some areas household-use-only permits are the norm, which affects what the land can be — a homesite, versus a place you can also water livestock. My [acreage guide on wells, water, and septic](/blog/buying-acreage-in-northern-colorado-wells-water-septic.html) goes deeper on this.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to get electricity to raw land?
paragraphs: Power is priced by distance. The serving utility (Xcel, Poudre Valley REA, or another co-op depending on where the parcel sits) quotes a line extension based on how far your build site is from their existing line, whether the run is overhead or underground, and the terrain in between. A parcel adjacent to a line might connect for surprisingly little; a beautiful site a long way up a canyon can carry a line-extension quote that changes the whole project's math.

The utility will give you a real estimate for a specific parcel — often free or for a modest engineering fee — and getting that quote BEFORE you buy is one of the smartest phone calls in land buying. Off-grid solar has also become a legitimate alternative worth pricing against a long line extension.

sections.h2: Septic, driveway, and the costs people forget
paragraphs: Septic starts with a soils/percolation evaluation; the result determines whether you can use a conventional system or need an engineered one, which costs significantly more. The county health department permits the system, and on resale Larimer County requires septic inspection and transfer paperwork — covered in my [Larimer land guide](/buying-land-larimer-co).

Then the quiet line items: driveway construction (length, grade, and drainage decide the price), a county access permit, site grading, and — in much of the Front Range foothills — wildfire-mitigation and defensible-space considerations that can affect insurance. None of these is a reason not to build; every one is a reason to price the specific parcel before you fall in love with it. Send me the listing and I'll help you build the real number.

faq: How much does it cost to build on unimproved land in Colorado?

The land-development portion — water, power, septic, access — is priced parcel by parcel: tap fees or well depth, distance to power lines, soil results, and driveway length each carry their own quote. Budget by collecting those four quotes for the specific parcel; any single all-in number you read online is a guess.
How much does it cost to get water and electricity on land?

Water: either your water district's current tap fee, or a well quoted per-foot by local drillers. Electricity: the utility's line-extension quote, driven by distance to their nearest line. Both quotes are parcel-specific and obtainable before you buy — get them during due diligence, not after closing.
Is it cheaper to buy raw land and build in Colorado?

Sometimes — but only when the development costs are known before you buy. Cheap land far from utilities often costs more all-in than dearer land next to them. The comparison only works with real quotes on both sides.
What is a perc test and why does it matter?

A soils evaluation that determines how the ground absorbs water — it decides whether standard septic works, an engineered system is required, or the site can't support septic at all. It's one of the first things to establish on any parcel without sewer service.
Can I put a well and septic on any Colorado land?

No — well permits depend on the parcel's water rights situation and state rules, and septic depends on soils and county health requirements. Both are checkable before purchase, and both belong in your contract contingencies.

/multi-generational-homes-for-sale-in-no.title: Multi-Generational & Next Gen Homes for Sale in Colorado: In-Law Suites, Guest Houses & More
/multi-generational-homes-for-sale-in-no.metaDescription: Multigenerational and Next Gen homes in Northern Colorado: what to look for, how builder 'home within a home' designs work, and how to search Loveland, Fort Collins, Greeley & Windsor for a home that fits the whole family.

sections.h2: What are 'Next Gen' homes?
paragraphs: 'Next Gen' is builder language — popularized as a trademarked 'home within a home' design — for a floor plan with a semi-independent suite: typically its own entrance, bedroom, living space, kitchenette, and laundry inside the main home. Other builders sell the same idea under names like multi-gen, dual living, or casita plans. In Northern Colorado's newer communities around Windsor, Severance, Timnath, and Greeley, these plans appear regularly in new construction.

On the resale market the same function hides under different labels: in-law suite, mother-in-law quarters, walkout basement with second kitchen, carriage house, or a property with a permitted ADU. That's why searching only the phrase 'next gen homes for sale' misses most of the real inventory — the right search is by FEATURES, which is exactly how I set up my clients' searches.

sections.h2: What to check before buying a multi-generational home
paragraphs: Function first: a true multi-gen setup needs real separation — its own entrance and bath at minimum, ideally kitchen facilities and laundry — plus accessibility if aging parents are part of the plan: a main-floor suite, minimal steps, wide doorways. Half-finished 'could be a suite' spaces are negotiating points, not solutions.

Rules second: if the second kitchen or separate unit matters to your plan, confirm how it's classified — some towns and HOAs regulate ADUs and rentals differently than an attached suite used by family. I check this during showings so a family doesn't fall in love with a layout the rules won't let them use as intended. Start with the [multi-generational buyer's guide](/guides/multi-generational-homes-northern-colorado.html), then [search current Northern Colorado listings](/search-homes.html) and tell me who the home needs to hold — I'll build the feature search that finds it.

faq: What is a Next Gen home?

A builder floor plan containing a semi-independent suite — separate entrance, living space, kitchenette, often laundry — inside the main house, designed for parents, adult children, or long-term guests. Several Northern Colorado builders offer versions under different names.
Are there multi-generational homes for sale in Colorado right now?

Yes, but they hide under many labels: next gen plans in new construction, in-law suites, basement apartments, and homes with ADUs or guest houses on resale. A feature-based search catches what a keyword search misses — that's how I run them for clients.
Is a mother-in-law suite the same as an ADU?

Not legally. A suite is part of the main dwelling; an ADU is a separately permitted dwelling unit, with rules that vary by town — affecting rentals, utilities, and sometimes resale value. Which one fits depends on how your family will actually use it.
Do multi-generational homes cost more?

Purpose-built plans and homes with true second suites carry a premium over comparable single-suite homes, but shared among two households the math often beats running two separate homes — and Northern Colorado's inventory spans a wide price range. Tell me your combined budget and I'll show you what it buys.
Which Northern Colorado towns are best for multi-generational living?

Newer communities in Windsor, Severance, Timnath, and Greeley carry the most purpose-built plans; Loveland and Fort Collins offer more resale homes with in-law setups and walkout-basement suites. The right town depends on the family's work, schools, and care needs — that's a conversation, and I'm happy to have it.

/day-trips-from-loveland-co.title: Things To Do in Loveland, CO & The Best Day Trips From Town
/day-trips-from-loveland-co.metaDescription: A local's list: the best things to do in Loveland, Colorado — art, trails, lakes, downtown — plus the scenic drives and day trips that make living here worth it, from Estes Park to the Poudre Canyon.

sections.h2: Things to do in Loveland itself — a local's short list
paragraphs: Before you leave town, know what's here: Loveland is Colorado's sculpture town — Benson Sculpture Garden alone holds well over a hundred pieces, and the annual sculpture shows draw artists nationally. Downtown's Fourth Street has become a genuine evening out — galleries, restaurants, the restored Rialto Theater. Outdoors, Boyd Lake State Park covers the water side; Devil's Backbone Open Space is the town's signature hike, that rock spine you see on half of Loveland's postcards; and the Loveland Recreation Trail loops the town for easy rides.

Seasonally: Valentine's season is Loveland's whole identity — the Sweetheart City remailing program stamps thousands of valentines every February — plus summer's outdoor concerts and the corn maze and pumpkin season out on the county roads. Living here means the 'day trip' question is often answered without starting the car — which, for what it's worth, is a big part of why my family stays.

sections.h2: The scenic drives worth a tank of gas
paragraphs: From Loveland you're positioned for some of the state's best drives: US-34 up the Big Thompson Canyon to Estes Park and Rocky Mountain National Park's alpine tundra; the Poudre Canyon (CO-14) west of Fort Collins, a state scenic byway tracing a wild and scenic river; the Peak to Peak Highway between Estes Park and Nederland for aspen season; and Horsetooth Reservoir's ridge roads for a sunset closer to home. Trail Ridge Road through the national park — the highest continuous paved road in the country — is the bucket-list one; it closes seasonally, so check before you go.

If you're weighing a move here, these drives are honestly part of the value of a Northern Colorado address — the mountains are a decision, not a vacation. When you're ready to look at what living here costs, [start a Loveland home search](/search-homes.html?cities=Loveland&noFloor=true) or read my [guide to which Northern Colorado town fits you](/blog/moving-to-northern-colorado-which-town-actually-fits.html).

faq: What is Loveland, Colorado known for?

Art — it's one of the country's notable sculpture towns — plus its Sweetheart City valentine tradition, Devil's Backbone Open Space, and its position as the gateway to the Big Thompson Canyon and Estes Park.
What are the best free things to do in Loveland?

Benson Sculpture Garden, Devil's Backbone and the Loveland Recreation Trail, downtown's public art and galleries, and lake evenings at North Lake Park cost nothing. Boyd Lake State Park charges a state-park pass.
What's the best day trip from Loveland?
Estes Park and Rocky Mountain National Park, forty-five minutes up the Big Thompson Canyon — with the Poudre Canyon a close second for a quieter, wilder river drive.
Is Loveland a good place to live?

I'm biased — I live here and sell homes here — but the combination of art scene, trail access, lakes, and a genuinely revived downtown at Northern Colorado prices is why people who visit keep asking me about listings.

/buying-land-larimer-co.title: Buying Land in Larimer County: Septic Transfers, Wells, Zoning & What To Check First
/buying-land-larimer-co.metaDescription: Buying land or rural property in Larimer County? What the septic transfer requirement means at sale, how well permits work, what open zoning allows, and the due-diligence list locals use.

sections.h2: Larimer County septic transfer: what it means when property changes hands
paragraphs: Larimer County requires septic systems to be inspected and brought through a transfer process when a served property sells — the county's program requires an inspection by a qualified inspector, repairs of identified deficiencies, and a transfer acceptance document, so a failing system gets caught at the sale instead of surprising the new owner a year later. The county's health department publishes the current requirements and fees; because program details evolve, check larimer.gov or ask us to verify the current process before you set a closing timeline.

Practically, this shapes both sides of a deal: sellers of septic-served property should schedule the inspection early — a required repair found late can push a closing — and buyers should read the inspection report as due-diligence gold, since it tells you the real condition of a system that costs serious money to replace. I build the septic timeline into every rural Larimer contract I write so it never becomes the thing that delays keys.

sections.h2: Wells and water rights on Larimer County land
paragraphs: If the parcel isn't served by a water district, the well permit is the heart of your due diligence: Colorado's Division of Water Resources issues permits by type, and what kind a parcel can get — household-use-only versus domestic with irrigation and livestock — depends on its water rights situation. An existing well should come with its permit, and its type needs to match how you plan to live; my [acreage water guide](/blog/buying-acreage-in-northern-colorado-wells-water-septic.html) walks through the permit types and the questions to ask.

Zoning rounds out the picture — much of rural Larimer sits in the county's Open zone district, covered in my [open zoning explainer](/understanding-open-zoning-in-larimer-county). Zoning, water, septic, and access: get those four answered and you actually know what you're buying. I help buyers run that whole checklist before they commit — bring me a parcel and we'll run it together.

faq: What is the Larimer County septic transfer program?

A requirement that septic systems be inspected and pass through a county transfer process when the property sells, so deficiencies are found and fixed at the transaction. The county publishes current rules and fees — verify them when you set your contract dates, as programs change.
Who pays for the septic inspection when selling in Larimer County?

It's negotiable in the contract, though sellers commonly handle the inspection and required repairs since the obligation attaches to the sale. What matters most is scheduling it early enough that a repair doesn't push the closing.
Do I need a well permit to buy land in Larimer County?

The land carries the permit situation — what you need is to verify what permit exists or what type the parcel could get from the Colorado Division of Water Resources, and whether that matches your plans for the property. Household-only versus domestic-with-livestock is a very different rural life.
Can I build a house on land I buy in Larimer County?

Usually the question is what and where, not whether: zoning district rules, setbacks, septic feasibility, access, and (in the foothills) wildfire considerations all shape it. Those answers exist before you buy — pulling them together is exactly the due diligence I run with land buyers.

/can-you-build-a-shop-barn-or-guest-hous.title: Can You Build a Shop, Barn, or Guest House on Your Land in Colorado? Permits & Rules
/can-you-build-a-shop-barn-or-guest-hous.metaDescription: What Colorado rural landowners can actually build: shop and barn permit basics, horse barn requirements, guest house and ADU rules, and the parcel checks to run before you pour concrete.

sections.h2: Horse barn requirements in Colorado: the short version
paragraphs: For most unincorporated Northern Colorado parcels, a horse barn is an accessory agricultural building — generally permitted where zoning allows keeping horses, but still subject to the county's building permit rules, setbacks from property lines and wells, and in some cases size thresholds that change the review level. Whether you need a full building permit can depend on the structure's size and use — counties treat a loafing shed differently than a barn with power, water, and living space — so the county building department's current rules for your parcel are the real authority.

Plan the practical layer too: manure management and drainage matter near wells and streams, and if a future buyer will care about the horse setup (in Northern Colorado, they will), building to what the market expects — safe fencing, water to the barn, all-weather access — pays you back at resale. If you're buying land with a barn already on it, permit history is a due-diligence question worth asking.

sections.h2: Guest houses and ADUs: when a second dwelling is allowed
paragraphs: A shop or barn is an accessory building; a guest house someone sleeps in is a DWELLING, and counties regulate those much more closely. Whether your parcel can have one — as a guest house, a full accessory dwelling unit, or not at all — comes down to its zone district's rules on second dwellings, minimum parcel sizes, and sometimes whether the unit can be rented. Water matters here too: a household-use well permit may not cover a second dwelling, which surprises a lot of would-be builders.

The pattern for all of it: your county's land use code plus a conversation with Planning, parcel number in hand, before money moves. If the ability to build a shop, barn, or guest quarters is the REASON you're buying a piece of land, make it a contingency — I write land contracts that way so my buyers aren't betting the purchase on an answer we could have gotten first.

faq: Can I build a shop on my property in Colorado?

On most rural parcels yes, as a permitted accessory building — subject to setbacks, size rules, and a building permit depending on the structure. Confirm with your county's building department using your parcel number; rules differ between counties and zone districts.
What are the requirements for a horse barn in Colorado?

Zoning that allows horses, compliance with setbacks (including from wells), and building-permit requirements that scale with the barn's size and features. Counties publish these rules; verifying them for your parcel takes one call and beats guessing.
Can I build a guest house on my property?

Only if your parcel's zoning allows a second dwelling and its water situation supports one — guest houses and ADUs are regulated as dwellings, not sheds. Check the zone district rules and your well permit type before planning.
Do barns and shops add property value?

In Northern Colorado's rural market, well-built and properly permitted outbuildings are genuine value — especially horse setups done to market expectations. Unpermitted structures do the opposite at sale time, when they become the buyer's inspection issue.

sections.h2: The Weld County land checklist
paragraphs: Weld County land runs from irrigated farm ground to new-community edge parcels, and the due diligence follows the same spine as anywhere in Northern Colorado — zoning, water, septic, access — with two Weld-specific emphases. First, mineral rights: much of Weld sits over active oil and gas, and knowing what's severed, what's leased, and where any facilities or setbacks fall relative to your building site is fundamental to both value and daily life. Second, water: in a county built on irrigated agriculture, what water (if any) conveys with the land — shares, taps, or well rights — can matter more than the acreage number.

USDA $0-down financing also reaches many Weld towns' surroundings — a real path to acreage for buyers who assume land means cash. The rules on wells, septic, and building mirror what I've written for [Larimer County](/buying-land-larimer-co) with Weld's own code and health department as the authorities; bring me a parcel and we'll run the checklist against the county's current rules together.

faq: Is Weld County a good place to buy land?

It offers some of Northern Colorado's most attainable acreage, with strong towns like Windsor, Severance, and Eaton growing around it. The value question is parcel-specific — water, minerals, access, and zoning decide it, and all four are checkable before you offer.
What about oil and gas rights on Weld County land?

Assume nothing conveys until title work says otherwise — mineral estates in Weld are commonly severed from the surface. What's beneath, who leases it, and where facilities sit near your parcel belong in your due diligence, and I make sure they're in it.
Can I get USDA zero-down financing for Weld County land?

USDA financing applies to homes in eligible rural areas — including much of Weld outside the bigger towns — rather than bare land alone, and eligibility maps change. If owning acreage with a home is the goal, ask us to verify what's currently eligible; it's a path many buyers don't know they have.
